cards.info: What is the Multiplication Counting Principle?
cards.backInfo: The total outcomes for sequential independent steps is the product of the number of choices at each step.

cards.info: When does order matter in a counting problem?
cards.backInfo: Order matters when items are placed in distinct positions, such as specific job titles or rankings.

cards.info: When is order considered irrelevant in counting?
cards.backInfo: Order does not matter when items are selected as a single group or set where internal arrangement is irrelevant.
cards.imageMarkdown: ![A flowchart to decide between Multiplication Principle, Permutations, and Combinations.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/1e562aab-51c2-4eda-be6e-d0c822778adc-1786506240670-298.webp)

cards.info: What is the definition of a permutation?
cards.backInfo: A permutation is a specific arrangement of a set of items where the order is significant.

cards.info: What is the definition of a combination?
cards.backInfo: A combination is a selection of items from a set where the order of selection is not significant.

cards.info: How do you calculate $P(n, k)$ practically?
cards.backInfo: Multiply $k$ consecutive descending integers starting from $n$.

cards.info: How is $C(n, k)$ derived from a permutation?
cards.backInfo: Divide the number of permutations $P(n, k)$ by $k!$ (k factorial) to remove duplicate arrangements.

cards.info: Is $C(n, k)$ larger or smaller than $P(n, k)$?
cards.backInfo: For $k > 1$, $C(n, k)$ is always less than $P(n, k)$ because order is removed.

cards.info: What mistake occurs when items cannot be reused?
cards.backInfo: Failing to decrease the number of available options at each subsequent step in the Multiplication Counting Principle.

cards.info: What is the definition of $n!$ (n factorial)?
cards.backInfo: The product of all positive integers from $n$ down to 1.

cards.info: How do you find total outcomes for a sequence of independent steps?
cards.backInfo: Multiply the number of choices available at each individual step together.

cards.info: Why does assigning 'President' and 'Vice President' roles require a permutation?
cards.backInfo: Because the roles are distinct positions, meaning the order of selection matters.

cards.info: Why is choosing a 3-person committee considered a combination?
cards.backInfo: The members are an equal group where the internal arrangement does not matter.

cards.info: Which counting method applies when items are arranged 'left-to-right on a shelf'?
cards.backInfo: Permutations, because the specific order or position of the items is significant.

cards.info: Which counting method applies when selecting a 'set' of toppings for pizza?
cards.backInfo: Combinations, because the order in which the toppings are chosen is irrelevant.

cards.info: What is the first step to calculate $P(10, 3)$ without a formula?
cards.backInfo: Multiply 3 descending integers starting from 10: $10 \times 9 \times 8$.

cards.info: What must you do to a permutation to convert it into a combination?
cards.backInfo: Divide the permutation by the factorial of the number of items selected ($k!$).

cards.info: Why is $C(7, 3)$ smaller than $P(7, 3)$?
cards.backInfo: $C(7, 3)$ divides by $3!$ to remove duplicate arrangements of the same group.

cards.info: If items cannot be repeated, how do options change at each step?
cards.backInfo: The number of available options must decrease by one at each subsequent step.

cards.info: How can you verify if a selection problem requires a combination?
cards.backInfo: Check if swapping two selected items results in the exact same outcome.
